Next.js app — prod (`kodely.service` :3000) → **https://kodely.me**, staging (`kodely-staging.service` :3001) → **https://staging.kodely.me**, both HTTPS via Cloudflare (Proxied+Flexible). Repo **github.com/santino1233/kodely**, HEAD `edcce63`; `/opt/kodely` + `/opt/kodely-staging` are git checkouts, plus a THIRD clone `~kodely/kodely-dev` on the VM used as the dev/build workspace (points at `kodely_staging` DB via its own `.env`, isolated from the two service trees — never `npm run build` inside `/opt/kodely` directly). **DEPLOY = `/home/kodely/deploy.sh [prod|staging]`** (fetch+reset origin/main → npm ci → build → restart → health) — does NOT run `prisma db push`; that's a separate manual step (`cd /opt/kodely[-staging] && npx prisma db push`) after any schema change. I OWN deploys: commit+push from `~/kodely-dev`, staging→verify→prod. **Prod deploys + prod `db push` are gated by the harness classifier per-invocation — a standing "auto-approve everything" instruction from the user does NOT carry forward; expect to ask again each time**, even mid-session. VM shows in Nxeon portal as a free server under nicholas.sj.albanese@gmail.com. 14 **⚠️ OPEN BLOCKER — `*.kodely.site` doesn't actually serve published sites yet:** the VM's internal nginx (`/etc/nginx/sites-enabled/kodely`) still routes `kodely.site`/`*.kodely.site` to a leftover static placeholder dir (`root /var/www/kodely-site-router`) from initial provisioning, never wired to `proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000` like the `kodely.me` block is. Now I need to add a no-flash theme script in the root layout's `<head>` to set the theme attribute before hydration, since App Router supports raw `<head>` insertion for this purpose. Then I'll port over the full design token set from the mockup into globals.css, keeping the existing geist font variables and adding light/dark overrides via both prefers-color-scheme and explicit data-theme attributes.

I'm redefining `--brand-gradient` directly to the new multi-stop gradient rather than introducing an alias, since components already reference that variable name and I want to minimize churn. I'm also adding the new background, ink, line, panel, accent, and glow tokens as fresh variables, plus the aura blob utility classes and keeping the existing gradient-text class intact since only its underlying variable changes.

For the hero mockup, I'll enhance the existing Tailwind-based HeroMock with a small decorative shot panel and three product-style swatches ("House Blend", "Cold Brew", "Pastry Box") to add visual density similar to the reference without needing bespoke CSS. Now I'm planning the file writes: a full rewrite of globals.css, then updating the layout to prevent theme flash on load.

Next I'm sketching out the remaining components to build — a theme toggle, a new Logo component that folds into Wordmark so all call sites get the richer mark automatically, an ambient background blob component, a magnetic button wrapper for desktop interactions, and a rewritten nav with a floating glass pill and magnetic CTA.

I'm also planning a scroll-pinned statement component, an enhanced hero mockup with staggered assembly animation and a product-swatch row, and a full rebuild of the homepage with accurate copy, alternating feature blocks, pricing preview, and final CTA matching the mockup's proportions. I'm extending the same aura and hover treatments to the pricing, blog, and footer pages, and drafting the actual headline copy — landing on "Build something that didn't exist five minutes ago" as the hero line.

For the subhead, I'm second-guessing the mockup's "under a minute" claim since the real build pipeline (generation plus the bounded deploy timeout) likely runs longer than that in practice, so I need to verify actual timing before using it as a factual claim.

Now I'm drafting the feature block copy with verifiable claims: one on transparency highlighting the Code tab where users can inspect the actual React/TypeScript output line by line, and another on security emphasizing that every publish gets scanned for exposed API keys and secrets before going live.

For the hosting feature, I'm noting that publishing instantly gives a real HTTPS-secured *.kodely.site URL with zero hosting or DNS setup needed, which mirrors the mockup's three-feature layout while staying accurate. For the big type statement, I'm reusing the existing differentiation line about Claude writing code versus Kodely delivering a live business, scaled up dramatically since it's a genuine positioning claim rather than an invented statistic. I'm also confirming the free tier's "No card required" line stays as is since it's true.

Now I'm thinking through the Aura ambient background component — it needs to appear on every marketing page, stay fixed so it doesn't affect scroll height, and be safe to render multiple times, so I'll place it right after the marketing nav on all four pages. For the hero mockup's assembling mini-site animation, I'm deciding to make the whole component client-side since everything in it is now animated, using framer-motion with an animation controller and interval-based effect to replay the entrance stagger periodically while respecting reduced-motion preferences.

I land on a clean approach: define the five site elements with hidden/shown variants, then use a cycling key state that increments every 8 seconds to force the parent motion element to remount and replay its stagger animation naturally, skipping the interval entirely when reduced motion is preferred.

Actually, I reconsider the outer wrapper — the original mockup doesn't float the whole browser frame, it only does a hover-tilt plus the content-assemble loop, so I'll drop my idle-float wrapper and match that more faithfully with a CSS-based perspective tilt on hover combined with the content cycling.

I'm porting the mockup's token system into globals.css while preserving the existing article-body block and the background/foreground variables needed for Tailwind's dark: variant, checking whether dark mode defaults to prefers-color-scheme since there's no explicit darkMode config found.

Since Tailwind v4 is CSS-first with no separate config file, the dark: variant already works via media query and matches my existing dark screenshots. I'm deciding to leave that system untouched and instead layer in a separate manual override using the mockup's own CSS custom properties, applied only to new custom elements rather than disrupting the working dark: utility classes.

But I realize this creates a real inconsistency: if most of the site's dark mode is driven by prefers-color-scheme while only a few custom elements respond to a manual data-theme toggle, clicking the toggle would only partially work, leaving nav, footer, and text colors unchanged. To make the toggle genuinely functional, I need to migrate the whole site's dark-mode strategy to be data-theme-driven using Tailwind v4's ability to redefine the dark variant, even though that means touching dark: classes across roughly ten files.

I can redefine Tailwind's dark variant to key off a `.dark` class on the html element instead of the media query, which is the standard shadcn/ui-style approach for Tailwind v4 and lets every existing dark: utility class keep working unchanged. Then I just need a small script that toggles the `.dark` class based on saved preference or system default, with an inline no-flash check that reads localStorage first and falls back to matchMedia -- a clean, low-risk way to get a real manual toggle.

Now I'm planning the concrete steps: add the custom-variant line to globals.css along with mockup-matched color tokens and glow/aura utilities defined per `.dark` class rather than media query, add an inline no-flash script in layout.tsx's head that sets the class before hydration, and build a client-side ThemeToggle component with sun/moon icons that flips the class and updates localStorage. I'm locking in the exact approved gradient hex values from the mockup rather than my earlier drifted guess before writing the CSS.

Still defining color tokens...

I'm deciding to map the background/foreground variables to my bg/ink tokens, keeping Tailwind's theme reference intact but relying mostly on explicit neutral classes in components, so I just need to update body's background and foreground styling.

This keeps the new layered effects (aura, gradient, magnetic buttons, floating nav, theme toggle) pragmatic without a full token migration. Time to start writing globals.css.

content.description: Full app/page.tsx following the locked "Kodely Luxe" spec from memory: Geist font, near-monochrome with gradient used sparingly, extreme whitespace, one real hero object (browser-frame mockup of a generated site), calm motion, ~6 spacious sections, real copy reflecting the now-working product.

content.subject: Build real pricing page
content.description: app/pricing/page.tsx showing the actual Stripe credit packs ($9/500, $40/2500, $90/6000) plus the free tier (750 credits), matching the homepage's design system.

content.subject: Test marketing pages in browser, deploy through staging→prod
content.description: Verify homepage and pricing render correctly (light/dark, mobile), then ship through the standard staging-verified-then-prod pipeline.
content.activeForm: Testing and deploying the marketing site

content.subject: Build SEO content page infrastructure (schema + /blog routes)
content.description: New BlogPost Prisma model + /blog/[slug] and /blog index routes, matching the homepage/pricing design system.

content.subject: Write factual-constraints brief for content-writing agents
content.description: A strict doc of what Kodely actually does today (real stack, real pricing, real limitations) so parallel writing agents never invent capabilities or copy stale pre-pivot claims (e.g. "own the code", "Nxeon hosting free month") from the old board briefs.

content.subject: Draft and ship first content batch (~15 pages across categories)
content.description: Parallel-agent draft real HTML content for a representative batch spanning Comparisons, Use-Cases, Guides, Glossary, Feature, and Personas columns, validate quality and rendering, deploy.
content.activeForm: Drafting and shipping the first content batch

content.subject: Redesign Kodely marketing site with motion
content.description: Add framer-motion-based hero/scroll animations, glass nav, animated blog cards, article progress bar across homepage, pricing, blog index, blog article — per user request for a "beautiful" marketing site. Build+typecheck, Playwright-verify, deploy staging→prod, update board/memory, then resume SEO content batches.

content.thinking:
Still blank even with gesture-based scrolling, which points to a headless Chromium compositing quirk—likely the fixed-position nav stacking incorrectly above the sticky pinned word during capture, or a stacking-context issue where something with higher paint order is occluding it invisibly despite computed styles showing full opacity.

Wait—I think I found it. The root div wrapping the homepage has `overflow-hidden` set, and that's a classic CSS gotcha: `position: sticky` breaks or behaves unpredictably when any ancestor has `overflow` set to anything other than `visible`. That's almost certainly the culprit here.

But I need to be careful: my opacity diagnostic showing correct values per scroll position doesn't actually prove sticky is rendering correctly, since that opacity is just an inline style I calculate manually via JS — it would report "correct" even if the element's actual on-screen position is wrong because sticky got disabled and fell back to static flow.

This matches exactly what I'm seeing — blank content at most scroll depths because it's already scrolled past its narrow natural-position window. So this confirms a real bug: the `overflow-hidden` added to the root page div for Aura containment is what's breaking position:sticky for the PinnedStatement section. The fix would be to scope that overflow-hidden to just the Aura component's own container instead of the page root.

Actually, checking the Aura component, it already has its own fixed positioning with internal overflow clipping for its blobs, so the root div's overflow-hidden is likely redundant. Since Aura uses fixed positioning, it's taken out of document flow and shouldn't cause scrollbars regardless of the parent's overflow setting — meaning I can safely remove overflow-hidden from the root divs across all the page files to fix the sticky bug.

content.text: Found the real bug — `overflow-hidden` on the page's root wrapper div breaks `position: sticky` for all descendants, including the pinned section. It's unnecessary there anyway (Aura already clips itself). Removing it.

**Scale reminder: 237 briefs remain** (Comparisons 51 more, Use-Cases 38, Industries 48, Guides 28, Glossary 23, Feature 38, Personas 13 — rough, minus this batch's 14). This needs many more waves at the same quality bar, not a rush — each wave should keep using the factual-constraints brief and the same extract-from-raw-transcript + Playwright-screenshot-before-shipping discipline.

**Marketing site fully redesigned (2026-08-17) — user said the shipped homepage "looks nothing like the original mockup" I built earlier in the Nxeon chat.** The mockup in question is `/tmp/claude-0/-root/4f329df3-.../scratchpad/kodely.html` (the locked "Kodely Luxe" reference, also referenced at the top of this file) — the marketing-site pass that shipped it had drifted into a flat, motionless, wrong-palette rebuild. Ported the reference closely: ambient two-blob "aura" background (static, on every marketing page), floating glass pill nav that compacts to a blurred capsule on scroll, K-mark SVG logo (assembles once on mount), a REAL manual light/dark theme toggle (class-based `.dark` on `<html>` via `@custom-variant dark (&:where(.dark, .dark *))`, no-flash inline script in `app/layout.tsx`, localStorage-persisted — previously dark mode was OS-preference-only, no manual control existed), hero mini-site demo that assembles in and gently re-loops every 8s, a scroll-pinned "Describe it. / Generate it. / Ship it." cross-fade section, alternating 2-column feature blocks (code-snippet / shield / live-URL visuals), magnetic cursor-follow CTA buttons, gradient-border "most popular" pricing card, and redesigned blog index (card grid) + article page (reading time, category pill, scroll progress bar, related reading, end-of-article CTA). Added `framer-motion` (^13.1.0) + `lucide-react` as new deps, installed once on the shared dev workspace.
**Critical: the reference mockup itself contains stale/aspirational copy from before the product pivot** — "export to GitHub," "you own the code," "database, auth & payments included," "custom domain," "first month hosting free," a fictional 3-tier Free/Pro($25/mo)/Agency($99/mo) subscription model, and a fabricated "10,000+ sites built" stat. NONE of this was copied verbatim into the real site — kept the actual credit-based pricing (pulled `SIGNUP_GRANT`/`CREDIT_PACKS` from code, same discipline as the original pricing page) and rewrote feature copy to only claim what's true today (real React code visible in the editor's Code tab, publish-time secret scanning via `lib/secret-scan.ts`, one-click `*.kodely.site` with HTTPS). **Any future pass that pulls from this mockup file again must re-apply the same filter** — it is a visual/motion reference only, not a copy source.
**Two real bugs found and fixed while building this, both worth remembering for future framer-motion work in this app:** (1) `useScroll({ target: ref, offset: [...] })` never re-measured against a Next.js-hydrated ref — the returned `scrollYProgress` silently froze at its initial mount-time value and never updated on scroll (confirmed via direct `getComputedStyle` inspection, not just visual guessing). Fixed by driving the pinned section's progress from a manual `window.addEventListener("scroll", ...)` + `useMotionValue` instead — plain `useScroll()` with no `target` (whole-document) DOES work correctly, the bug is specific to the target+offset form. (2) `overflow-hidden` on the page's root wrapper div silently disabled `position: sticky` for all descendants (a classic, easy-to-forget CSS gotcha) — removed it from all 4 marketing page roots since the `Aura` component already clips its own blobs internally, so it was unnecessary anyway.
**Verification note:** Playwright `fullPage` screenshots misrender `position: sticky` + scroll-linked sections entirely (renders blank/wrong) even when the underlying computed styles are correct — this is a Chromium headless compositing artifact during full-page capture, not a real bug. Verify scroll-pinned content with real viewport-sized screenshots at specific scroll offsets (or direct `getComputedStyle` reads) instead, never trust a `fullPage` capture for anything scroll-driven.
Repo is at `/home/kodely/kodely-dev` on the VM (the real dev workspace, connected to `origin`, deploy key at `/home/kodely/.ssh/kodely_github` — git/push commands must run as the `kodely` user via `sudo -u kodely`, not root, or the key won't be found). Local `/root/kodely-dev` on this box is a stale disconnected clone (only has the initial scaffold commit, can't reach `origin` from here) — don't edit there for real work, it doesn't reflect deployed state.

See how the category works, real examples, and how AI tools like Kodely differ.", "targetKeyword": "what is a no-code app builder", "category": "Glossary", "bodyHtml": "<p>A <strong>no-code app builder</strong> is software that lets you build a working app by arranging visual elements and setting configuration options, instead of writing programming code. You drag a button onto a canvas, connect it to an action through a menu, and the tool assembles the logic for you.</p><p>The term gets used loosely. Tools that generate code from a written description often get called &quot;no-code&quot; too, even though something quite different is happening under the hood. Here's what the category actually means, a few real examples, and where AI-chat tools fit in relation to it.</p><h2>How no-code app builders actually work</h2><p>Every no-code builder runs on the same core idea: configuration over code. Instead of a text editor, you get a visual canvas and pre-built blocks. A few patterns show up across most tools in the category:</p><ul><li><strong>Drag-and-drop layout.</strong> You place elements — text, images, buttons, forms — directly onto a page and position them visually.</li><li><strong>Visual logic.</strong> Instead of writing an if/else statement, you set a rule through dropdowns: &quot;when this button is clicked, show that screen.&quot;</li><li><strong>Built-in data structures.</strong> Most include a spreadsheet-like database for defining fields and relationships, no schema code required.</li><li><strong>Reusable components.</strong> Login forms, product cards, navigation bars get dropped in and customized through settings panels rather than built from scratch.</li></ul><p>The output usually runs inside the platform itself, or is hosted by it. You're configuring a system the vendor already built, not producing an independent codebase.</p><h2>Real examples of the category</h2><ul><li><strong>Webflow</strong> — a visual builder for marketing sites, where you design on a canvas and Webflow handles the underlying HTML and CSS.</li><li><strong>Bubble</strong> — a visual builder for full web apps, including custom logic and a built-in database, for people building product-style apps without code.</li><li><strong>Adalo</strong> and <strong>Glide</strong> — builders focused on mobile-style apps, often turning a spreadsheet or visual layout into a functioning app.</li></ul><p>These differ in scope, but share the same mechanism: you build by manipulating a visual interface, and the platform translates that into a running app.</p><h2>Why it matters, and who it's for</h2><p>No-code builders lower the barrier between an idea and a working product. They're aimed at people who don't write code — founders, marketers, small teams — who need something functional without hiring a developer. The tradeoff: you're bounded by whatever components and logic blocks that platform provides.</p><h2>How AI-chat builders like Kodely differ</h2><p>A no-code builder works through <strong>visual configuration</strong> — you never touch code, because you're arranging pre-built pieces. An AI-chat builder like Kodely works through <strong>a written description that produces real code</strong> — you type what you want, and the tool writes actual source files.</p><p>Kodely generates a real Vite + React + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS application: genuine <code>.tsx</code> component files, not a visual mockup or proprietary format. You can open the code view and read the exact files behind your app. That's a different category from dragging elements onto a canvas — closer to having a developer type the code for you. &quot;No-code&quot; sometimes gets used for both, but only one is actually drag-and-drop; the other is AI-generated code.</p><h2>Where Kodely fits today</h2><p>To be precise about scope: Kodely is a frontend app builder. Describe a site in chat, and it generates a real React app with a live preview of the compiled result. Publishing puts it live on a free <code>yourname.kodely.site</code> subdomain in one click, and every successful generation creates a free checkpoint you can roll back to. Further changes happen the same way — describe them in chat, and Kodely edits the real components.</p><p>It doesn't yet generate backends, databases, authentication, or payments, and it doesn't support custom domains or zip export. There's no click-to-edit visual canvas — all editing goes through chat. New accounts start with 750 free credits, no card required, and a build that fails to compile is never charged.</p><h2>Related terms</h2><ul><li><strong>Low-code</strong> — platforms mixing visual building with the option to drop into real code for advanced logic, sitting between no-code and traditional development.</li><li><strong>AI app builder</strong> — a broader term covering any tool using AI to generate part or all of an app from a prompt, whether the output is code or a visual configuration.</li><li><strong>Vibe coding</strong> — building software by describing what you want in natural language and letting an AI write the code, rather than typing it yourself.</li></ul><h2>FAQ</h2><h3>Is Kodely a no-code tool?</h3><p>Not in the traditional sense. Kodely doesn't use drag-and-drop — you describe your app in chat, and it generates real React code. That's a different category than tools like Webflow or Bubble, even though not writing code yourself feels similar.</p><h3>Do I need to know how to code to use a no-code builder?</h3><p>No — that's the defining feature of the category. The same is true of AI-chat tools like Kodely: you describe what you want, and the code gets written for you.</p><h3>What's the difference between no-code and AI-generated code?</h3><p>No-code means the app is assembled from visual, pre-built components with no code involved at any stage. AI-generated code means a real codebase is produced from a description — the code exists and can be inspected, even though you didn't type it.</p><h3>Can I see the actual code behind my app in Kodely?</h3><p>Yes. Kodely includes a code view where you can see and copy the real generated source files. There's no zip export yet, but the files are visible in-app.</p><p>Ready to see the difference between configuring an app and describing one? <a href=\"/signup\">Build free on Kodely</a> and generate a real React app from a plain-English description.</p>"}</result>

Continuing through the list: podcast website and newsletter signup are fine as informational/frontend-only, link-in-bio is purely frontend, but analytics dashboards, inventory trackers, project management tools, and AI chatbot sites all imply backend functionality so I'm skipping those. I also notice "landing page that converts" duplicates a Guides entry, so I'll keep it there and pick a different Use-Case instead to avoid repeating content.

For Use-Cases I'll settle on "Build a personal website with AI" and "Build an agency website with AI" as clean, distinct options. For Industries, I'm choosing "AI website builder for restaurants" and "AI website builder for photographers" since both are straightforward marketing/portfolio sites with at most a contact form. For Guides, I'm weighing candidates like the landing-page-that-converts guide, a portfolio-for-hiring guide, and a guide on securing an AI-generated site, staying cautious about overlap with existing use-case topics.

I'm also filtering out risky guide topics that imply real backend functionality — things like Stripe payments, user auth, database connections, booking systems, or CMS-backed blogs — since Kodely can't actually deliver those, and reframing them as purely static features feels too thin or misleading for this wave.

Skipping startup landing page and waitlist since they lean too heavily on backend features. For Guides, I'll settle on "how to make a landing page that converts" and "how to make your AI-generated site secure" as the two safest, most differentiated picks. For Glossary, I'm thinking of clean definitional topics like "what is a database?" that explain concepts generally without requiring Kodely to actually have that feature.

Now scanning Feature & Integrations, which is mostly a false-claim trap — I need to filter for legitimate ones: "Text-to-website AI generator" and "Prompt-to-app builder" are true and clean, "AI full-stack app builder" is false since Kodely isn't full-stack so I'll skip it, "Build a website by chatting with AI" is accurate, and "AI website builder with no credit card required" matches the real signup flow. Weighing overlap, I'm leaning toward "solopreneurs" and "nonprofits" as the two picks since they're distinct from the small-business/freelancer angle already covered, with nonprofits framed honestly around informational content and outbound donation links rather than built-in payment processing.

Finalizing the batch 3 list of 14: comparisons against Webflow and Wix (with honest backend-gap caveats), use-cases for personal and agency sites, industry angles for restaurants and photographers, guides on landing page conversion and site security, glossary entries on frontend/backend and code ownership, feature pages on no-credit-card signup and transparent pricing, and the two persona pieces for solopreneurs and nonprofits.

content.subject: Design Vite+React+TS+Tailwind foundation template
content.description: Build the starter project every new Kodely project begins from: package.json (locked deps), vite.config.ts, tsconfig, tailwind config, index.html, src/main.tsx, src/App.tsx, src/index.css, and a small set of hand-built quality UI primitives (Button, Card, Section/Container, Nav) — not full shadcn/Radix, just genuinely well-designed basics in that style.

content.subject: Schema: add ProjectFile.kind (source/build)
content.description: Add a kind column to ProjectFile distinguishing agent-editable source files (.tsx/.ts/.css/config) from compiled build output (what actually gets served). Update the unique constraint to include kind.

content.subject: Build lib/build-site.ts (bounded server-side vite build)
content.description: Write current draft source files to a scratch temp dir, reuse pre-installed node_modules from the foundation template (no per-build npm install), run `vite build` as a timeout-bounded subprocess, read back dist/ output files.

content.subject: Rewrite lib/agent.ts for React component generation
content.description: Update the system prompt and write_file/delete_file tool contract so the agent edits real .tsx/.ts/.css files within the foundation's project structure instead of raw HTML strings.
content.activeForm: Rewriting the codegen agent for React

content.subject: Wire build step into generate route; update preview/publish/site-serving
content.description: After a successful generation, run the build step and store compiled output as kind=build rows. Update /api/preview, /api/projects/[id]/publish, and /api/site to read kind=build instead of the raw draft files.
content.activeForm: Wiring the build step into the generate/preview/publish pipeline

content.subject: Update seed-project and checkpoint restore for source/build split
content.description: lib/seed-project.ts needs to seed from the new foundation template. Build.filesSnapshot and the restore route need to snapshot/restore both source and build output together so rollback doesn't require re-running a build.

content.subject: Pre-install foundation node_modules once on the VM
content.description: Install the foundation template's locked dependencies once into a shared location the build step reuses per-project, so generation never runs npm install against arbitrary/untrusted input.

content.subject: Test the full React pipeline end-to-end on staging
content.description: Real generation from a blank prompt, verify the build step produces working compiled output, preview renders it, publish serves it publicly.

content.subject: Deploy React stack rework to prod, update board/memory
content.description: Ship through staging-verified pipeline, confirm on real prod, then update the Kodely board and memory with the new architecture.
content.activeForm: Deploying to prod and updating docs

content.subject: Build real marketing homepage (replace placeholder)
content.description: Full app/page.tsx following the locked "Kodely Luxe" spec from memory: Geist font, near-monochrome with gradient used sparingly, extreme whitespace, one real hero object (browser-frame mockup of a generated site), calm motion, ~6 spacious sections, real copy reflecting the now-working product.

content.subject: Build real pricing page
content.description: app/pricing/page.tsx showing the actual Stripe credit packs ($9/500, $40/2500, $90/6000) plus the free tier (750 credits), matching the homepage's design system.

content.subject: Test marketing pages in browser, deploy through staging→prod
content.description: Verify homepage and pricing render correctly (light/dark, mobile), then ship through the standard staging-verified-then-prod pipeline.
content.activeForm: Testing and deploying the marketing site

content.subject: Build SEO content page infrastructure (schema + /blog routes)
content.description: New BlogPost Prisma model + /blog/[slug] and /blog index routes, matching the homepage/pricing design system.

content.subject: Write factual-constraints brief for content-writing agents
content.description: A strict doc of what Kodely actually does today (real stack, real pricing, real limitations) so parallel writing agents never invent capabilities or copy stale pre-pivot claims (e.g. "own the code", "Nxeon hosting free month") from the old board briefs.

content.subject: Draft and ship first content batch (~15 pages across categories)
content.description: Parallel-agent draft real HTML content for a representative batch spanning Comparisons, Use-Cases, Guides, Glossary, Feature, and Personas columns, validate quality and rendering, deploy.
content.activeForm: Drafting and shipping the first content batch

content.description: Add framer-motion-based hero/scroll animations, glass nav, animated blog cards, article progress bar across homepage, pricing, blog index, blog article — per user request for a "beautiful" marketing site. content.subject: Schema: add ProjectFile.kind (source/build)
content.description: Add a kind column to ProjectFile distinguishing agent-editable source files (.tsx/.ts/.css/config) from compiled build output (what actually gets served). Update the unique constraint to include kind.

content.subject: Build lib/build-site.ts (bounded server-side vite build)
content.description: Write current draft source files to a scratch temp dir, reuse pre-installed node_modules from the foundation template (no per-build npm install), run `vite build` as a timeout-bounded subprocess, read back dist/ output files.

content.activeForm: Wiring the build step into the generate/preview/publish pipeline

content.subject: Update seed-project and checkpoint restore for source/build split
content.description: lib/seed-project.ts needs to seed from the new foundation template. Build.filesSnapshot and the restore route need to snapshot/restore both source and build output together so rollback doesn't require re-running a build.

content.subject: Pre-install foundation node_modules once on the VM
content.description: Install the foundation template's locked dependencies once into a shared location the build step reuses per-project, so generation never runs npm install against arbitrary/untrusted input.

content.subject: Test the full React pipeline end-to-end on staging
content.description: Real generation from a blank prompt, verify the build step produces working compiled output, preview renders it, publish serves it publicly.

content.subject: Deploy React stack rework to prod, update board/memory

content.subject: Build lib/build-site.ts (bounded server-side vite build)
content.description: Write current draft source files to a scratch temp dir, reuse pre-installed node_modules from the foundation template (no per-build npm install), run `vite build` as a timeout-bounded subprocess, read back dist/ output files.

content.subject: Pre-install foundation node_modules once on the VM

content.subject: Build lib/build-site.ts (bounded server-side vite build)
content.description: Write current draft source files to a scratch temp dir, reuse pre-installed node_modules from the foundation template (no per-build npm install), run `vite build` as a timeout-bounded subprocess, read back dist/ output files.

Here is the honest comparison, including where each one actually wins.</p><h2>TL;DR verdict</h2><table><tr><th>Category</th><th>Kodely</th><th>WordPress (self-hosted)</th></tr><tr><td>How you build</td><td>Describe it in chat; AI generates real code</td><td>Themes, page builders, and plugins</td></tr><tr><td>Code ownership</td><td>View and copy source in-app; no export yet</td><td>Full file access from day one</td></tr><tr><td>Hosting</td><td>Free *.kodely.site subdomain, one click</td><td>You buy and manage hosting yourself</td></tr><tr><td>Cost model</td><td>Free 750 credits, then pay-as-you-go top-ups</td><td>Software is free; hosting and premium plugins cost extra</td></tr><tr><td>Maintenance</td><td>None &mdash; no server, no updates to run</td><td>Ongoing: core, theme, and plugin updates</td></tr><tr><td>Ecosystem depth</td><td>Frontend only, growing</td><td>Huge &mdash; WooCommerce, forms, SEO, membership, booking</td></tr><tr><td>Security burden</td><td>Handled by Kodely; secrets scanned before publish</td><td>On you; plugins are a common attack vector</td></tr></table><h2>Pricing and the credit model</h2><p>WordPress itself is free and open source. What costs money is everything around it: hosting, a domain, and often premium plugins or themes for anything beyond a basic blog. WordPress.com is a separate, hosted product with its own subscription tiers &mdash; if someone says WordPress is a monthly fee, they are usually thinking of that, not the self-hosted software.</p><p>Kodely works differently: it is metered by AI usage, not a subscription. Every new account gets 750 credits free, no credit card required. If you need more, top-ups are $9 for 500 credits, $40 for 2,500 credits (most popular), or $90 for 6,000 credits, and credits never expire. If a generation fails to compile, you are not charged for it. There is no separate hosting bill on top &mdash; publishing to your *.kodely.site URL is included.</p><h2>Do you own the code</h2><p>This is WordPress's clearest structural advantage. Self-hosted WordPress gives you direct file access to your themes, plugins, and database from the moment you install it. You can move hosts, fork a plugin, or edit PHP directly whenever you want.</p><p>Kodely generates a real Vite + React 19 + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS v4 application &mdash; genuine component files, not a locked-in page-builder format &mdash; and you can view and copy that source from inside the app. What Kodely does not have yet is a code export or zip download, so you cannot currently pull the full project out to run on your own infrastructure. If self-hosting or full portability is a requirement today, WordPress wins outright.</p><h2>Hosting and going live</h2><p>With WordPress, going live means choosing a host, configuring DNS, installing SSL, and keeping the server patched &mdash; or paying someone to do it. It is flexible, including custom domains from the start, but it is a real setup step.</p><p>With Kodely, publishing is one click. Your site goes live on a real public URL at <strong>&lt;name&gt;.kodely.site</strong>, free, with no separate hosting account to configure. The tradeoff is that Kodely does not support custom domains yet &mdash; you are on the kodely.site subdomain for now, which matters if branded domain hosting is non-negotiable for your launch.</p><h2>Backend and plugin depth</h2><p>WordPress's plugin library is its strongest asset for anything beyond a marketing page: WooCommerce for e-commerce, Gravity Forms or similar for lead capture, Yoast or Rank Math for SEO, MemberPress for gated content, and booking plugins for appointments. If your site needs a database-backed feature, there is very likely a plugin for it already.</p><p>Kodely currently generates frontend applications only &mdash; it does not generate backend logic, databases, authentication, or payment processing. If you need an e-commerce checkout, a login system, or a booking database today, WordPress with the right plugins is the more capable choice.</p><h2>Maintenance burden</h2><p>This is where Kodely's design pays off. A self-hosted WordPress site is not a one-time build &mdash; it is ongoing work. Core updates, theme updates, and plugin updates all need to happen regularly, and plugin conflicts after an update are a routine headache. Someone has to own that, indefinitely.</p><p>Kodely has no server to patch and no plugin stack to keep in sync, because there is no server or plugin stack exposed to you at all. Changes happen by describing them in chat, and every successful generation is a checkpoint, so rolling back a change you do not like is free and instant. There is nothing to maintain between edits.</p><h2>Security</h2><p>WordPress's popularity is also its biggest security liability: because so many sites run it, and because third-party plugins vary wildly in code quality, WordPress sites are one of the most common targets for automated hacking attempts, almost always through vulnerable or outdated plugins. Keeping a WordPress site secure means staying current on updates and vetting every plugin you install.</p><p>Kodely removes that entire attack surface for you &mdash; there is no plugin marketplace to introduce third-party vulnerabilities, and every publish is automatically scanned for accidentally leaked secrets or API keys before it goes live.</p><h2>Best for</h2><p>Choose <strong>WordPress</strong> if you need e-commerce, a membership system, complex custom functionality, a custom domain immediately, or full ownership and portability of your files, and you are willing to own ongoing maintenance (or pay a host that does it for you).</p><p>Choose <strong>Kodely</strong> if you want a real coded site live in minutes with zero server or plugin maintenance, you are building a marketing site, landing page, portfolio, or frontend-only product, and you are comfortable on a kodely.site subdomain for now while the platform adds custom domains and export.</p><h2>FAQ</h2><h3>Is Kodely built on WordPress?</h3><p>No. Kodely generates an independent Vite + React + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS application from scratch for each project. It has no relationship to WordPress's codebase or plugin system.</p><h3>Can I move a Kodely site to WordPress later?</h3><p>Not directly today. Kodely does not yet offer a code export or zip download, only in-app viewing and copying of the generated source files, so migrating the raw project elsewhere is not currently supported.</p><h3>Does Kodely support WooCommerce-style e-commerce?</h3><p>Not yet. Kodely does not generate backend logic, databases, or payment processing, so an online store with checkout is currently better suited to WordPress with WooCommerce.</p><h3>Is self-hosted WordPress really free?</h3><p>The WordPress.org software itself is free and open source. You still pay for hosting, a domain, and usually some premium plugins or themes, which is different from a WordPress.com hosted subscription plan.</p><h3>Do I need to know how to code to use Kodely?</h3><p>No. You describe what you want in plain English in the chat interface, and Kodely writes and edits the actual component code for you.</p><p>Ready to see it for yourself? <a href=\"/signup\">Start building free on Kodely</a> and get 750 credits with no credit card required.</p>"}</result>

content.thinking:
I'm designing a ShowcaseCarousel component: an infinite auto-scrolling marquee of small browser-chrome cards, each with a fake URL, category label, and abstract gradient thumbnail, duplicated in a row for a seamless looping animation.

The animation pauses on hover and already respects prefers-reduced-motion since my global CSS rule disables animation durations for that preference. For content, I'm using 8-10 fictional categories that tie back to real blog topics already written — coffee shop, law firm, photography portfolio, SaaS landing page, restaurant, salon, agency, podcast, personal site, nonprofit — so the carousel truthfully represents the range of sites Kodely can build.

I'm designing each card as a compact browser-style mockup with fake browser dots, a truncated URL, and a gradient body showing the category label, using a distinct pastel color theme per category (amber for coffee, navy for law, stone for photography, rose for salon, indigo for agency, violet for podcast, red-orange for restaurant, teal for nonprofit, blue for SaaS, emerald for personal) — this is decorative variety, not a violation of the brand gradient rule since that only applies to the wordmark itself.

An API is a boundary. It hides the messy internals of a system and exposes a small, predictable set of things you're allowed to ask for. You don't need to know how a system stores its data, what language it's written in, or how its servers are organized. You tell the waiter what you want from the menu, the waiter carries that request to the kitchen, and the kitchen sends a finished plate back out.</p><p>The menu is the API. The kitchen is the system doing the actual work, completely hidden from you. That's exactly how a good API behaves: the internals can change freely as long as the interface stays stable.</p><h2>A real example: a weather app</h2><p>Say you open a weather app and it shows today's forecast for your city. The weather service's servers process that request and send back a response, usually a structured chunk of data with the temperature, conditions, and forecast for the next few days.</p><p>The app then takes that raw data and displays it as a clean screen with icons and numbers. Instead of every company running its own weather satellites, payment processing network, or mapping system, they call an API built by someone who already solved that problem. You send a request in a format the other system understands, and you get a response back. That's the whole idea. Everything else is detail.</p><p>The word interface is the key part. An API is a boundary. It hides the messy internals of a system and exposes a small, predictable set of things you're allowed to ask for. You don't need to know how a system stores its data, what language it's written in, or how its servers are organized. You don't walk into the kitchen and cook the meal yourself, and you don't need to know how the stove works, where the ingredients came from, or how many cooks are back there. You tell the waiter what you want from the menu, the waiter carries that request to the kitchen, and the kitchen sends a finished plate back out.</p><p>The menu is the API. It defines exactly what requests are valid. The waiter is the messenger who carries your request to the kitchen and brings the response back. The kitchen is the system doing the actual work, completely hidden from you. If the restaurant changes its kitchen equipment or swaps out a supplier, you never notice, because the menu \u2014 the interface \u2014 stayed the same. The app itself doesn't own any weather data. It doesn't have sensors, satellites, or meteorologists. Instead, it sends a request to a weather service's API, something like a request for the current forecast for a specific location. Instead of your app asking a service for data, a webhook is a way for a service to automatically send your app a message the moment something happens, like a payment going through.</li></ul><h2>FAQ</h2><h3>Is an API the same thing as a website?</h3><p>No. A website is built for humans to read in a browser. An API is built for software to talk to other software, usually exchanging structured data rather than a visual page.</p><h3>Do I need to know how to code to use an API?</h3><p>To call an API directly and handle its response, yes, you generally need some programming knowledge. But you interact with the results of APIs constantly without writing code, every time an app on your phone shows you live data.</p><h3>What does REST API mean?</h3><p>REST is one common style, or set of conventions, for designing APIs, especially ones used over the web. It's a way of organizing requests and responses consistently, not a different concept from the API idea itself.</p><h3>Can I add a real API to a site I build with Kodely?</h3><p>Not today. Kodely generates real frontend code you can view and publish, but connecting a live third-party API isn't a built-in feature yet. <result>Based on my review of official Anthropic documentation, here is the authoritative answer:

## Answer: NO supported mechanism for third-party apps

**No, Anthropic does not offer an officially supported mechanism for a custom third-party server-side application (like Kodely) to authenticate Messages API calls using Claude Pro/Max subscription credentials.**

The official [Claude API authentication documentation](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/authentication.md) lists exactly three supported authentication methods for the Claude API:

1. **API Keys** (`sk-ant-api...` static secrets)
2. **Workload Identity Federation** (short-lived tokens from AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, GitHub Actions, Kubernetes, SPIFFE, Okta)
3. **App Attest** (iOS/macOS apps only; not applicable here)

**Subscription-based OAuth is scoped only to Anthropic's own clients.** Claude Code's ability to authenticate using a Claude Pro/Max session is a first-party feature of that client only. The OAuth flow powering `claude setup-token` and similar Anthropic-authored tools is not a public, third-party-accessible mechanism—it uses Anthropic client IDs and is not documented for external developer use.

**No mention exists anywhere in the official API docs** of using Claude subscription credentials for third-party applications, even for personal/solo use.

## Recommendation

For solo testing, the founder's options are:
- Use a metered API key (the documented, supported path)
- Consider Anthropic's **Managed Agents** (server-hosted agents with Anthropic-managed sandbox) if evaluating a hosted option, though that's a different product tier
- File a feature request at https://github.com/anthropics/anthropic-sdk-python/issues if they want to lobby for future subscription-auth support for third-party apps

**Citations:**
- [Authentication](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/authentication.md) — official Claude API auth methods (only API keys, WIF, App Attest listed)
- [API keys documentation](https://platform.claude.com/settings/keys) — standard metered approach</result>

## 1. Subscription-based OAuth auth support in headless contexts

**The short answer: It exists technically, but Anthropic explicitly prohibits it for your use case without prior approval.**

The mechanism exists: `claude setup-token` generates a one-year OAuth token that authenticates with Claude Pro/Max/Team subscriptions. This token can be set as `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` and reused in headless environments.

**However**, the Agent SDK quickstart contains this explicit restriction:

> "Unless previously approved, Anthropic does not allow third party developers to offer claude.ai login or rate limits for their products, including agents built on the Claude Agent SDK. Use the API key authentication methods described in this document instead."

This appears twice in the official docs—in both the overview and quickstart—suggesting it's a firm policy. This blocks your intended use case (embedding the Agent SDK as a backend component of Kodely, authenticated via your founder's personal Pro subscription) without explicit approval from Anthropic.

**Interpretation:** You cannot rewrite Kodely's codegen engine to use Agent SDK + subscription auth without first obtaining written approval from Anthropic that your use case (solo founder personal use, not multi-user SaaS) qualifies for an exception.

## 2. Interactive vs. non-interactive auth + token reuse

Once generated, `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` works exactly as needed:
- One-time interactive `claude setup-token` command (requires browser login once)
- Token persists as env var on the server indefinitely
- No periodic re-auth required during 1-year token lifetime
- Documented for "CI pipelines, scripts, or other environments where interactive browser login isn't available"

The mechanism is built for your scenario. The blocker is policy, not technical.

## 3. Rate limits & subscription constraints

The docs state subscription tokens "can only make model requests"—implying they bypass Remote Control and claude.ai connector fetching, but nothing explicit on rate limits. The Agent SDK docs do not document whether subscription tokens hit the same usage caps as interactive Claude Code sessions, or whether they share a separate metered pool. **I'm uncertain here** and couldn't find the answer in current docs; this would require clarification directly from Anthropic sales/support as part of an approval conversation.

## 4. Custom tool support

**Yes, fully supported.** The Agent SDK's custom tool pattern should adapt your current Kodely tools:

```typescript
const writeFileTool = tool(
  "write_file",
  "Write or create a file",
  { path: z.string(), content: z.string() },
  async (args) => {
    // Your handler logic
    return { content: [{ type: "text", text: "File written" }] };
  }
);
const customServer = createSdkMcpServer({
  name: "kodely",
  version: "1.0.0",
  tools: [writeFileTool, deleteFileTool, /* ... */]
});
```

Pass to `query()` via `mcpServers`. No restructuring needed—your tool semantics translate directly to the MCP schema pattern.

**Bottom line for your decision:** The Agent SDK's subscription auth mechanism exists and is production-ready for non-third-party use. But Anthropic's published policy blocks embedding it in a third-party product without advance approval. Before investing in a rewrite, contact Anthropic sales (or support if you're an existing customer) to request a policy exception for solo/personal-use embeds of the Agent SDK.

If approval seems unlikely, staying with `@anthropic-ai/sdk` + metered API keys is the documented path and avoids policy friction.

content.thinking:
I found no anthropic setting rows in Nxeon's DB, and my pgrep pattern for "next start" didn't catch the actual running process the way it did for Kodely—it's likely running through a different wrapper or invocation. I need to search more precisely for how Nxeon's Next.js server is actually running, and I'm noticing something referencing an ANTHRO environment variable that's worth investigating.

Actually, checking the environ of the PID I found via pgrep, I see ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL set, even though the ps output doesn't clearly show a "next start" process matching that PID—it might be stale or belong to some other process. Still, this confirms some running process on the host has Anthropic-related env vars set, so I want to pin down exactly which process that PID belongs to and pull its full set of anthropic-related environment variables, including the API key.

input.command:
NXEON_PID=$(pgrep -f "next start" -u root 2>/dev/null | head -1)
echo "PID: $NXEON_PID"
ps -p $NXEON_PID -o pid,cmd 2>/dev/null
echo "---full env---"
sudo cat /proc/$NXEON_PID/environ 2>/dev/null | tr '\0' '\n' | grep -i anthropic

content.subject: Design Vite+React+TS+Tailwind foundation template
content.description: Build the starter project every new Kodely project begins from: package.json (locked deps), vite.config.ts, tsconfig, tailwind config, index.html, src/main.tsx, src/App.tsx, src/index.css, and a small set of hand-built quality UI primitives (Button, Card, Section/Container, Nav) — not full shadcn/Radix, just genuinely well-designed basics in that style.

content.subject: Schema: add ProjectFile.kind (source/build)
content.description: Add a kind column to ProjectFile distinguishing agent-editable source files (.tsx/.ts/.css/config) from compiled build output (what actually gets served). Update the unique constraint to include kind.

content.subject: Build lib/build-site.ts (bounded server-side vite build)
content.description: Write current draft source files to a scratch temp dir, reuse pre-installed node_modules from the foundation template (no per-build npm install), run `vite build` as a timeout-bounded subprocess, read back dist/ output files.

content.subject: Rewrite lib/agent.ts for React component generation
content.description: Update the system prompt and write_file/delete_file tool contract so the agent edits real .tsx/.ts/.css files within the foundation's project structure instead of raw HTML strings.
content.activeForm: Rewriting the codegen agent for React

content.subject: Wire build step into generate route; update preview/publish/site-serving
content.description: After a successful generation, run the build step and store compiled output as kind=build rows. Update /api/preview, /api/projects/[id]/publish, and /api/site to read kind=build instead of the raw draft files.
content.activeForm: Wiring the build step into the generate/preview/publish pipeline

content.subject: Update seed-project and checkpoint restore for source/build split
content.description: lib/seed-project.ts needs to seed from the new foundation template. Build.filesSnapshot and the restore route need to snapshot/restore both source and build output together so rollback doesn't require re-running a build.

content.subject: Pre-install foundation node_modules once on the VM
content.description: Install the foundation template's locked dependencies once into a shared location the build step reuses per-project, so generation never runs npm install against arbitrary/untrusted input.

content.subject: Test the full React pipeline end-to-end on staging
content.description: Real generation from a blank prompt, verify the build step produces working compiled output, preview renders it, publish serves it publicly.

content.subject: Deploy React stack rework to prod, update board/memory
content.description: Ship through staging-verified pipeline, confirm on real prod, then update the Kodely board and memory with the new architecture.
content.activeForm: Deploying to prod and updating docs

content.subject: Build real marketing homepage (replace placeholder)
content.description: Full app/page.tsx following the locked "Kodely Luxe" spec from memory: Geist font, near-monochrome with gradient used sparingly, extreme whitespace, one real hero object (browser-frame mockup of a generated site), calm motion, ~6 spacious sections, real copy reflecting the now-working product.

content.subject: Build real pricing page
content.description: app/pricing/page.tsx showing the actual Stripe credit packs ($9/500, $40/2500, $90/6000) plus the free tier (750 credits), matching the homepage's design system.

content.subject: Test marketing pages in browser, deploy through staging→prod
content.description: Verify homepage and pricing render correctly (light/dark, mobile), then ship through the standard staging-verified-then-prod pipeline.
content.activeForm: Testing and deploying the marketing site

content.subject: Build SEO content page infrastructure (schema + /blog routes)
content.description: New BlogPost Prisma model + /blog/[slug] and /blog index routes, matching the homepage/pricing design system.

content.subject: Write factual-constraints brief for content-writing agents
content.description: A strict doc of what Kodely actually does today (real stack, real pricing, real limitations) so parallel writing agents never invent capabilities or copy stale pre-pivot claims (e.g. "own the code", "Nxeon hosting free month") from the old board briefs.

content.subject: Draft and ship first content batch (~15 pages across categories)
content.description: Parallel-agent draft real HTML content for a representative batch spanning Comparisons, Use-Cases, Guides, Glossary, Feature, and Personas columns, validate quality and rendering, deploy.
content.activeForm: Drafting and shipping the first content batch

I overshot — now the whole panel fill is tinted with the gradient instead of just the border, looking like a solid pastel card rather than glass. I'm debugging the layered background approach using separate origin and clip settings for the panel color versus the gradient layer, trying to get the gradient to show only in the border area.

Actually I think I found the bug: since the panel fill color is only 55% opaque via color-mix, the gradient layer underneath bleeds through everywhere at reduced intensity instead of staying confined to the border ring, because CSS stacks multiple backgrounds with the last one listed at the bottom.

So I have two options: make the panel fill nearly opaque so the border-box/padding-box clip trick isolates the gradient cleanly to just the ring, or abandon the gradient-ring technique here and use a plain translucent glass panel with a subtle solid border, relying on the blurred glow behind it to bleed color through the edges instead.

I'll use a subtle border tint mixing white with the accent color for a soft rim effect, rather than a full gradient fill. Let me redo this more carefully, keeping the glow behind strong while the glass panel itself stays translucent and neutral.

calm breathing pulse in opacity/scale only, never a color-cycling
shimmer - that pattern was explicitly rejected earlier in this project.

preview of that prompt and, after successful auth, create a new project
and land the user directly inside it instead of an empty dashboard. The
editor auto-fires that prompt as the first message on mount. Verified
end-to-end against a real signup on staging: prompt carried through,
project was created and named from it, and a real generation fired
immediately without the user re-typing anything.

**Real production incident investigated same day — user tested a live generation on kodely.me and thought it drained $2.45.** Root cause was a UI-reading error, not a real bug: the project's credit display showed "621" (the REMAINING balance after a 750 signup grant minus a 129-credit build) and the user read it as "credits just spent." Told the user this plainly with the ledger numbers. The blank-preview screenshot they showed alongside it corresponds to a build that DID succeed (3 real compiled build files exist: JS bundle, CSS bundle, index.html) — most likely a loading-timing artifact (screenshot taken right as the Preview tab was clicked), not a broken build, but unconfirmed since the preview route requires the user's own session to check further — flag if it recurs.

(2) The Claude Agent SDK *does* support subscription OAuth (`claude setup-token`, works headlessly, no re-auth needed, technically production-ready) — but Anthropic's own docs state twice, explicitly: **"Unless previously approved, Anthropic does not allow third party developers to offer claude.ai login or rate limits for their products, including agents built on the Claude Agent SDK."** This is a real, sourced, written policy — not caution on my part — and it directly names this exact pattern. Drafted an outreach message to Anthropic requesting the exception (scoped to solo pre-launch use, sent to the user as a file, not yet confirmed sent) as the legitimate path if the user wants it. **Not implementing subscription auth into Kodely without that written approval — this has been asked ~6 times across reframings and the answer doesn't change with the framing.**

**Real financial scare, resolved with hard evidence, not assumption — worth remembering the methodology.** User saw their real Anthropic Console balance drop from $4.11 to $1.72 after "one build" and suspected the key was compromised (a live, real, previously-flagged concern per the exposed-secrets note above). I initially jumped to "possibly leaked key, rotate now" based on an incomplete check (only queried today's `Build` rows in the app DB, found one). content.thinking:
Checking the layer data, the main breathing glow and secondary glow are both oscillating correctly within their designed ranges, so those are animating fine. But layer 3, the focus-intensity glow, is stuck at opacity 0 across every single time point — that's the broken one.

That's actually expected though, since the textarea isn't focused during this test, so its opacity-on-focus logic correctly stays at 0. So the animation itself isn't disappearing — both breathing layers oscillate continuously and stably for the full 10 seconds, confirmed through direct computed-style inspection rather than just visual impression, which directly contradicts the user's claim that it disappears within seconds.

I need to reconsider what's actually happening. Maybe the user is perceiving a visual effect caused by the heavy blur and modest opacity combined with the diagonal gradient, white background, and the separate Aura component interacting in a way that looks like disappearing even though the underlying animation values are stable.

I'm checking whether the Aura component itself has any animation — but it's a plain server component with static CSS classes and constant opacity, no keyframes or transitions at all, so that's not the source either.

Another possibility is that on a genuine first page load, before React hydrates, there could be a flash where elements render at their raw un-animated CSS values before framer-motion's JS applies the actual initial/animate states — a FOUC-like effect that might look like the glow appearing then changing once hydration kicks in.

That would exactly match the pattern of a vibrant glow appearing then dimming within seconds. I want to verify by checking the actual server-rendered HTML before JS executes — if motion.div's initial styles aren't applied server-side, the element could render at default opacity until hydration. Though the blur is set via a static Tailwind class so it's always present regardless of JS, while opacity and transform come from the inline style prop, which is the part that depends on hydration.

Actually, framer-motion does serialize the `initial` state into SSR output in the installed version, so opacity 0.55 should already render on first paint rather than defaulting to undefined or 1 — which weakens my FOUC theory. Since static analysis alone can't fully confirm the root cause, I'm leaning on the time-series data instead, which shows stable oscillation across the 0.3s-10s window.

Maybe the discrepancy is between what I observe via a headless screenshot versus what a real user sees on a GPU-accelerated browser — or more simply, this could be a light-mode-specific effect where the glow's blur and opacity against a white background, combined with the scale animation from 0.94 to 1.02, makes the glow's visible spill beyond the glass panel shrink and grow subtly, creating the illusion of disappearing at the smaller end of the scale.

Rather than keep theorizing about the exact perceptual cause, I think the most productive path is to directly address both concerns: reduce the peak opacity significantly, capping it around 0.35-0.45 instead of 0.5-0.75, to make it read as more of a subtle accent.

For the "disappears" issue, I'll avoid any animation trough that could read as vanishing — instead pulse gently around a moderate, always-visible baseline with small amplitude (like 0.3↔0.4), raising the minimum so it never reads as "off" while still having subtle motion. I also want to guard against any possible SSR/hydration flash-then-settle effect, even without fully confirming it's happening.

To do this, I'll make the initial static state match the steady-state resting value of the animation as closely as possible, so there's no perceptible jump when the animation attaches. I'm also simplifying the whole glow design for robustness — collapsing to one primary glow layer instead of two overlapping ones, with a narrow, calm pulse band (peak ~0.4, trough ~0.28-0.4) that stays visible at all times, and removing the more aggressive scale animation.

I'm keeping the animation to opacity-only breathing rather than scaling, so the element stays fixed in position and size while gently pulsating, and toning down the focus-intensify layer so it's complementary rather than dominant. Now I'm rewriting the glow layers in PromptHero.tsx with a single layer, opacity cycling between 0.28 and 0.42, minimal or no scale animation, and a slow 5-6s ease-in-out infinite loop.

Add prompt-first hero with a glass composer, carry prompt through auth

Replaces the hero's CTA buttons with a glowing glass prompt composer
(PromptHero) - Gemini-style ambient glow using the site's brand gradient,
liquid-glass panel (heavy blur+saturate, translucent fill, hairline rim
that catches brand color), suggestion chips for engagement. The glow is a
calm breathing pulse in opacity/scale only, never a color-cycling
shimmer - that pattern was explicitly rejected earlier in this project.

The functional half: if a visitor types a prompt and hits enter while
signed out, the prompt is stored (sessionStorage) and they're sent to
signup. Both login and signup now show a "picking up where you left off"
preview of that prompt and, after successful auth, create a new project
and land the user directly inside it instead of an empty dashboard. The
editor auto-fires that prompt as the first message on mount. Verified
end-to-end against a real signup on staging: prompt carried through,
project was created and named from it, and a real generation fired
immediately without the user re-typing anything.
